content: External cephalic version (ECV) is a procedure used to turn a fetus from a breech position to a cephalic (head-down) position before delivery. When performed at term (after 37 weeks of gestation), ECV has been shown to reduce the number of breech presentations and the need for cesarean sections. However, the success rates of the procedure remain relatively low. This review focuses on studies that initiated ECV before term, specifically before 37 weeks of gestation. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of starting ECV before term in reducing breech presentation at birth, influencing the method of delivery, and assessing its impact on preterm birth rates, perinatal morbidity, stillbirth, and neonatal mortality. To gather evidence, the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register was searched up to March 31, 2015, along with reference lists of relevant studies. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing ECV initiated before term with either no ECV or ECV performed at term. Cluster-randomized trials were eligible, but none were identified. Quasi-randomized trials and cross-over studies were excluded. Two independent reviewers assessed the trials for inclusion, evaluated the risk of bias, extracted data, and ensured accuracy. The quality of evidence for key outcomes was assessed using the GRADE approach. Five studies involving a total of 2,187 women were included in the review. Blinding of the intervention was not possible, and the impact of this lack of blinding on the outcomes is unclear. For other domains of bias, the studies were judged to have either low or unclear risk. One study compared ECV completed before 37 weeks with no ECV and found no significant difference in the rate of non-cephalic presentation at birth (risk ratio [RR] 1.04, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.64 to 1.69; 102 participants). Another study examined a policy of initiating ECV as early as 33 weeks and continuing up to 40 weeks, with the option to repeat the procedure until delivery. This study demonstrated a reduction in the rate of non-cephalic presentation at birth (RR 0.59, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.77; 179 participants). Three studies compared ECV initiated between 34 to 35 weeks with ECV started at 37 to 38 weeks. The pooled results indicated that early ECV reduced the risk of non-cephalic presentation at birth (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.74 to 0.90; 1,906 participants; high-quality evidence), failure to achieve vaginal cephalic birth (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.83 to 0.97; 1,888 participants; high-quality evidence), and vaginal breech delivery (RR 0.44, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.78; 1,888 participants; high-quality evidence). However, the difference in cesarean section rates between early and later ECV groups was not statistically significant (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.00; 1,888 participants; high-quality evidence). There was evidence that early ECV increased the risk of preterm labor compared to ECV performed after 37 weeks (6.6% in the early ECV group versus 4.3% in the control group; RR 1.51, 95% CI 1.03 to 2.21; 1,888 participants; high-quality evidence). No significant differences were observed between groups in terms of low Apgar scores at five minutes or perinatal death (stillbirth and neonatal mortality up to seven days), although the quality of evidence for these outcomes was low. In conclusion, initiating ECV before term reduces the likelihood of non-cephalic presentation at birth compared to no ECV. When compared to ECV performed at term, starting ECV at 34 to 35 weeks may offer benefits in reducing non-cephalic presentation and the risk of vaginal breech birth. However, early ECV is associated with an increased risk of late preterm birth. Future research should report on infant morbidity outcomes to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the risks and benefits. It is essential to have thorough discussions with pregnant women about the timing of ECV to enable informed decision-making.
